Discussion: Gallocyanin-chrome alum method will stain both DNA and RNA dark blue and, therefore, cannot provide a good estimate on the amount of DNA in the cell. The same is true for hematoxylin. Thioflavine S stain can be used to demonstrate amyloid deposition and must be visualized with a fluorescent microscope. It cannot be used to estimate the amount of DNA in tissue sections. Solochrome cyanine method can be used to differentiate osteoid from newly laid-down bone and older bone but does not stain DNA specifically. Feulgen reaction stains DNA red-purple and the cytoplasm green and is a widely accepted method to demonstrate DNA on histologic sections.
explanation: The Feulgen reaction is a widely accepted method to demonstrate DNA on histologic sections, as it stains DNA red-purple and the cytoplasm green, allowing for a clear distinction between DNA and other cellular components.

questionText: This is a portion of the cerebral cortex and white matter stained by modified Bielschowsky stain The findings being illustrated here are most consistent with:
options: "Swiss cheese" artifact due to gas production resulted from post mortem bacterial overgrowth.
The specimen has been fixed in formalin and then frozen (freezing artifact).
Over digestion by enzyme at the initial steps as required by modified Bielschowsky stain.

Wax cracks due to in proper processing of the tissue. E. Knife marks. Discussion: "Swiss cheese" artifacts can be generated by post mortem over growth of gas producing bacteria. The size can vary from millimeters to over 1 centimeters. Just like the vacuoles in Swiss cheese, their distribution is irregular and there is a significant variation in size. In contrast to the vacuoles being shown here, the vacuoles in "Swiss cheese" artifact have smooth margins. Although enzyme digestion can be used to retrieve signal in immunohistochemistry and in situ hybridization, it is not a required step for modified Bielschowsky stain which is a silver stain that is often used in the study of neuropathology. In addition, the holes that are created by over digestion is never so sharply defined. Wax cracks typically appear as irregular, elongated slits in the tissue section. Knife marks are straight, very long and often appear as parallel lines. These features are not present here. In the section being shown, there is a randomly regular distribution of vacuoles of comparable size in the grey matter. The extent of involvement is similar in different parts of the photo. There is also similar involvement in the white matter albeit the the vacuoles are far smaller. This difference is well appreciated in the medium magnification photo. This type of artifact is produced by freezing tissue that has been fixed in formalin. This brain has been fixed in formalin and solidly frozen before paraffin sections are made. This type of artifact can be avoided by cryoprotection with concentrated sucrose solution if frozen sections are to be done on formalin fixed tissue blocks.
explanation: The 'Swiss cheese' artifact is consistent with post-mortem bacterial overgrowth, which can cause gas production and create irregularly distributed vacuoles with smooth margins in the tissue, as seen in the cerebral cortex and white matter stained by modified Bielschowsky stain.

questionText: Which of the followings is not true for the succinate dehydrogenase preparation of muscle biopsy as illustrated here?
options: This preparation detects an enzyme that is present in both the mitochondria and tubules.
This preparation can be used to detect abnormal mitochondrial accumulation in mitochondrial diseases.
The substrate will turn blue if the enzyme is present in the biopsy tissue.

Type I fibers will stain dark and type II fibers will stain pale. E. This preparation can be used to demonstrate the core in central core disease. Discussion: In contrast to NADH-TR, succinate dehydrogenase is present only in the mitochondria
explanation: This preparation detects an enzyme that is present in both the mitochondria and tubules is incorrect because succinate dehydrogenase is present only in the mitochondria, not in the tubules. This preparation is used to detect abnormal mitochondrial accumulation in mitochondrial diseases and can be used to demonstrate the core in central core disease. Type I fibers will stain dark and type II fibers will stain pale.

questionText: The light and dark bands that are perpendicular to the long axis of the muscle fiber in this resin embedded, toulidine blue stained semi-thin (0.5-1 m) section are:
options: Caused by inhomogeneous curing of the block.

Caused by vibration of the block, the block holder, or the knife. E. Insufficient osmium concentration leading to softening of the block. Discussion: The ripple-like light and dark bands observe a rather strict periodicity and are perpendicular to cutting action of the ultramicrotome. This type of artifact is typically caused by a high frequency vibration of the cutting system that involves either the block, the block holder, or the knife. The vibration introduces a forward and backward type of movement of the block against the knife during sectioning. How to tell from this photo? There is a knife mark here (delineated by the white arrows). Knife marks are always perpendicular to the direction of movement of the block on sectioning. Knife marks are never this periodical nor this wide as illustrated here. Insufficient osmium or inappropriate curing will not lead to this type of artifact. Inhomogeneous staining will lead to rather distinct patches of under stained or unstained areas with a blur margin. On the other hand, there is a faint staining water mark due to suboptimal staining as illustrated by the red arrow. Please note the curvy shape of this water mark which reflects the rolling shape of the section because of the vibration artifact (red arrow). Also note that the section above this curvy line is slightly more darkly stained then the section below this line.
explanation: This periodic, ripple-like pattern is caused by high-frequency vibration of the cutting system during sectioning, resulting in a forward and backward movement of the block against the knife. This type of artifact is characterized by its periodicity and perpendicular orientation to the cutting action. It can be distinguished from knife marks, which are perpendicular to the direction of movement but not periodic.

questionText: Hematoxylin stain with progressive formulae:
options: Are widely used by many first year residents who want to make progress and be promoted to the second year.
Are used only by scientists who already had stellate achievements, such as getting the Nobel prize.
Are used to remediate medical students who have made no progress during their pathology rotation.

Are designed for the automatic staining machines so that slides racks can progress forward. E. Give a darker staining intensity with longer staining time. Discussion: The first four answers are obviously jokes. I hope they would serve as the spices of your day. In general, hematoxylin stains are divided into the so-called progressive formulae and regressive formulae. The progressive formulae stain far slower then that of the regressive formulae and therefore the staining intensity can be controlled by the length of the staining time. Hematoxylin stains with regressive formulae involve over staining the sections followed by a differentiation step to achieve the desired staining intensity. The regressive formulae are particularly useful for tissues that do not take up hematoxylin well. One of the best examples is over decalcified tissue.
explanation: Hematoxylin stains with progressive formulae allow for controlled staining intensity by varying the staining time, making them particularly useful for tissues that require precise hematoxylin uptake.

questionText: Which of the following is a confirmatory test for syphilis:
options: Wasserman test Feedback: The FTA-ABS is not intended for use as a screening test. It should only be used to differentiate between true positives, false positives, and in late or latent syphilis
explanation: The FTA-ABS (Fluorescent Treponemal Antibody Absorption) test is a confirmatory test for syphilis because it detects antibodies against the bacterium Treponema pallidum, which causes syphilis. It is used to differentiate between true positives, false positives, and in late or latent syphilis. This is in contrast to non-treponemal tests like RPR and VDRL, which can produce false positives due to other conditions.

questionText: The most likely cause of an elevated potassium level in an apparently normal individual is:
options: Interfering substances Feedback: Hemolysis could result from improper specimen collection technique, or improper storage.
explanation: Hemolysis is the most likely cause of an elevated potassium level in an apparently normal individual because it releases potassium from red blood cells into the plasma, artificially elevating the serum potassium concentration. This can occur due to improper specimen collection technique, such as using a needle with a syringe that is not designed for blood collection, or improper storage, which can cause red blood cells to rupture and release their contents.

questionText: Metabolic acidosis is characterized by:
options: High pH Feedback: Metabolic acidosis is the result of either:
explanation: Metabolic acidosis is characterized by an excess of acid or a deficiency of bicarbonate, leading to a decrease in blood pH. This results in a low pH, which is the defining feature of metabolic acidosis. The low pH disrupts normal cellular function and can have serious consequences if left untreated.

questionText: The Quelling test is useful for which of the following :
options: Isolation of various strains of Staphylococcus

Isolation of various strains of Streptococcus Feedback: Capsular swelling results from the addition of specific capsular antibody to an isolate of the organism. This test is generally not required for routine diagnosis.
explanation: The Quellung test is a serological typing method used to identify Streptococcus pneumoniae by observing the capsular swelling resulting from the addition of specific capsular antibody to an isolate of the organism.

questionText: The relative centrifugal force of a centrifuge may be affected by all except the following:
options: RPM Feedback: The amount of time a sample is spun does not affect the relative centrifugal force
explanation: The relative centrifugal force (RCF) is determined by the centrifuge's speed (in revolutions per minute, RPM) and the radius of the rotor. The amount of time a sample is spun does not affect the RCF, as it is a function of the acceleration due to the centrifugal force, which is independent of time.

questionText: Standard precautions means that:
options: Known infectious patients must be handled with extraordinary care
Mask, gloves and gowns should be worn in all hospital patient's rooms
All specimens must be handled as if they are hazardous and infectious
Always wash your hands before drawing a patient’s blood sample
explanation: Standard precautions in clinical laboratory medicine involve handling all specimens as if they are hazardous and infectious, emphasizing the importance of safety and minimizing the risk of exposure to potential pathogens. This approach is based on the principle of caution and is essential for protecting laboratory personnel and preventing the transmission of infectious agents. By adopting this mindset, laboratory professionals can maintain a safe working environment.

questionText: RDW is an indication of which of the following:
options: Microcytosis Feedback: Red Cell Distribution Width (RDW) is a mathematical expression of size variation used toquantify anisocytosis. The higher the RDW, the greater the anisocytosis. RDW is increased iniron deficiency, and tends to be normal in thalassemia. Increased RDW may be an early indication of iron deficiency, where it may precede the onset of microcytosis.
explanation: RDW is an indication of variability in red blood cell (RBC) volume, which is a measure of anisocytosis. An increased RDW value suggests a greater variation in RBC size, often seen in iron deficiency anemia before the onset of microcytosis.

questionText: Group A beta-hemolytic streptococci are best characterized by which of the following:
options: Bacitracin sensitivity Feedback: Group B streptococci are characterized by a positive cAMP test. Streptococcus pneumoniae is characterized by Optochin susceptibility Enterococci are positive by the bile- esculin test.
explanation: Group A beta-hemolytic streptococci are best characterized by their ability to hydrolyze bile esculin, which is a key differentiator from other streptococcal species. This is a critical identification feature in clinical laboratory settings. Bile esculin-hydrolysis is a test that detects the ability of bacteria to hydrolyze esculin in the presence of bile salts.

questionText: The turbidity of the bacterial inoculum of a standard disc diffusion (Kirby-Bauer)susceptibility test is:
explanation: The turbidity of the bacterial inoculum in a standard disc diffusion (Kirby-Bauer) susceptibility test is typically adjusted to 0.5 McFarland Standard to ensure a uniform bacterial density, allowing for accurate interpretation of the test results.

questionText: Which of the following is not a common support medium used in electrophoresis techniques:
options: Dextrose Feedback: Cellulose acetate and agarose gels are most commonly used in the clinical laboratory
explanation: Polyacrylamide gel is not commonly used in the clinical laboratory for electrophoresis techniques, as it is more often used in research settings due to its higher resolution and sensitivity. Cellulose acetate and agarose gels are preferred in clinical laboratories for their ease of use and sufficient resolution for diagnostic purposes. This makes polyacrylamide gel the correct answer as it is not a common support medium used in clinical electrophoresis.

questionText: The normal range for urine pH is:
explanation: The normal range for urine pH is typically between 4.6 and 8.0, as the kidneys regulate pH levels to maintain acid-base balance. A pH range outside of this normal range may indicate underlying conditions such as kidney disease or metabolic disorders. This range allows for the excretion of excess hydrogen ions or bicarbonate ions to maintain homeostasis.

questionText: Which of the following is not a likely cause of an abnormal thrombin time (TT):
options: Dysfibrinogenemia Feedback: The thrombin time is performed by adding thrombin to citrated plasma. It is prolonged by heparin, a deficiency or abnormality of fibrinogen and the presence of fibrin split products.Aspirin affects primarily platelet function.
explanation: Aspirin primarily affects platelet function, which does not directly impact thrombin time. Thrombin time is a measure of the conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin, and aspirin's effect on platelet aggregation does not interfere with this process.

questionText: What is the eight hour occupational exposure limit for a chemical called?
explanation: The Threshold Limit Value (TLV) is a concentration of a chemical in the air that is considered safe for an 8-hour workday and a 40-hour workweek. It is used to determine the maximum allowable concentration of a chemical in the workplace to prevent adverse health effects. The TLV is established by the American Conference of Governmental Industrial Hygienists (ACGIH).

questionText: Spherocytes are associated with which two of the following conditions:
options: Iron deficiency Feedback: Spherocytes result from removal of small amounts of erythrocyte membrane, with resultant reduction in surface to volume ratio. This may occur in the reticuloendothelial system, as inhereditary sherocytosis and autoimmune hemolytic anemia, or may be due to direct injury of red cells, as in patients with severe burns.
explanation: Hereditary spherocytosis is a genetic disorder characterized by the production of red blood cells that are sphere-shaped rather than the normal biconcave disk shape. This results from mutations in genes encoding proteins of the erythrocyte membrane, leading to removal of small amounts of membrane and a resultant reduction in surface to volume ratio. Spherocytes are also seen in autoimmune hemolytic anemia due to the removal of membrane-bound antibodies.

questionText: The generally accepted age range for homologous blood donation is:
options: Over the age of 14years Feedback: Prospective donors over 65 may be accepted at the discretion of the blood bank physician.Many donor centers safely involve elderly donors in their collection programs.
explanation: The generally accepted age range for homologous blood donation is 21-65 years due to the increased risk of blood-borne pathogens and other health issues in younger individuals, as well as the potential for decreased physical ability in elderly donors. However, some donor centers may accept donors over 65 at the discretion of the blood bank physician. This age range is based on clinical laboratory medicine standards to ensure the safety of both the donor and the recipient.

questionText: Which of the following organisms in most frequently associated with endocarditis:
options: Streptococci Feedback: Various Streptococci are the most common causes of endocarditis, although many otherorganisms have been implicated.
explanation: Various Streptococci are the most common causes of endocarditis due to their ability to form biofilms on heart valves, leading to infection and inflammation.

questionText: Ionized calcium is most commonly measured using which of the following method:
options: Color complex formation between calcium and o-cresolphthalein
explanation: Ionized calcium is most commonly measured using calcium ion selective electrodes because they directly measure the free, physiologically active form of calcium in the blood, which is essential for various physiological processes.

questionText: The prozone effect ( when performing a screening titer) is most likely to result in:
options: Mixed field reaction Feedback: Prozone effect (due to antibody excess) will result in an initial false negative in spite of the large amount of antibody in the serum, followed by a positive result as the specimen is diluted.
explanation: The prozone effect occurs when there is an excess of antibodies in the serum, leading to an initial false negative result due to the inability of the antibodies to bind to the antigen. As the specimen is diluted, the antibody concentration decreases, allowing for antigen-antibody complex formation and a positive result. This phenomenon is a result of the optimal antigen-antibody ratio being exceeded.

questionText: Which of the following tests on amniotic fluid would be included when assessing fetal maturity:
explanation: The L/S (lecithin/sphingomyelin) ratio is a key indicator of fetal lung maturity, as it reflects the ability of the lungs to produce surfactant. Bilirubin is also assessed in amniotic fluid to evaluate fetal hemolysis and potential liver function. This combination is crucial for determining fetal maturity.

questionText: Therapeutic hemapheresis may be used to treat all of the following except:
options: Cryoglobulinemia Feedback: Therapeutic Hemapheresis is the process of removing a harmful blood component, and returned the remaining blood components to the patient. The examples cited above are indications for plasmapheresis, in which plasma containing a harmful substance is removed from the body, and replaced with FFP or other volume expanders, depending on the patient's condition.
explanation: Therapeutic hemapheresis is not typically used to treat HIV infections, as it does not directly target the virus. Instead, antiretroviral therapy is the standard treatment for HIV. Hemapheresis may be used to manage complications related to HIV, but it is not a primary treatment for the infection itself.

questionText: A smear that is prepared from equal parts of methylene blue and whole blood will be used for:
options: Reticulocyte count Feedback: Remaining nuclear fragments found in reticulocytes take up the methylene blue dye.
explanation: The methylene blue dye stains the RNA in the reticulocytes, making them visible under a microscope. This allows for the identification and counting of reticulocytes, which is essential for assessing bone marrow activity and erythropoiesis. The remaining nuclear fragments found in reticulocytes take up the methylene blue dye, making them visible and aiding in the reticulocyte count.

questionText: Gram positive organisms
options: readily stain with safranin in the Gram stain Feedback: Gram positive organisms resist decolorization with acetone-alcohol. Gram negative organismsare decolorized, and subsequently stain with safranin.
explanation: Gram positive organisms resist decolorization with acetone-alcohol due to the thick peptidoglycan layer in their cell walls, which prevents the solvent from penetrating and removing the crystal violet stain. This characteristic is a key feature of the Gram staining technique, allowing for the differentiation of Gram positive and Gram negative bacteria. The peptidoglycan layer is absent or thinner in Gram negative organisms, making them susceptible to decolorization.

questionText: Which of the following are not appropriate indications for the use of fresh frozen plasm
options: Severe bleeding in the presence of significantly elevated PT secondary to vitamin K deficiency
Replacement component after plasma exchange in patients with TTP or HUS

Dilutional coagulopathy with significant active bleeding, and PT and PTT twice normal Feedback: Since each unit of fresh frozen plasma (FFP) carries with it the risk of transmitting blood bornepathogens, and other products which do not carry this risk are available, FFP should not be used as a volume expander
explanation: Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) should not be used as a volume expander due to the risk of transmitting blood-borne pathogens, and other products such as crystalloids or colloids are available for this purpose. FFP is typically reserved for situations where coagulopathy correction is necessary. This is in line with clinical laboratory medicine standards.

questionText: If a pipette is labeled (TC) " to contain " you would do the following:
options: Drain pipette, but not blow out
Drain contents then blow out or rinse
Drain to last mark on pipette
Do not consider the meniscus when filling Feedback: "TC" means the total volume contained in the pipette - you must blow out to remove total contents.
explanation: When a pipette is labeled 'TC', it indicates the total volume contained. To accurately measure this volume, the contents must be completely removed, which involves blowing out the pipette to remove any residual liquid. This ensures that the pipette is free of any remaining substance, allowing for accurate measurement.

questionText: The concentration of sodium chloride in an isotonic solution is :
options: 1molar Feedback: Isotonic or normal saline is a 0.85 % solution of sodium chloride in water.
explanation: Isotonic or normal saline is a 0.85% solution of sodium chloride in water, which means it has the same concentration of solutes as human blood. This concentration is essential for maintaining cellular integrity and preventing hemolysis. Isotonic solutions are used for various medical purposes, including wound cleaning and IV fluids.

questionText: The positive square root of the variance of a set of values is called:
explanation: The positive square root of the variance of a set of values is called the standard deviation, which is a measure of the amount of variation or dispersion of a set of values. It represents how spread out the values are from the mean value. In clinical laboratory medicine, standard deviation is an essential statistical parameter used to evaluate the reliability of laboratory results.

questionText: Patients with antibody to the following antigen are immune to Hepatitis B:
explanation: Patients with antibody to the surface antigen are immune to Hepatitis B because the presence of surface antibody indicates a past infection and subsequent development of immunity. This is due to the fact that surface antibodies are produced in response to the surface antigen, which is present on the surface of the Hepatitis B virus. The presence of surface antibody prevents the virus from entering liver cells and causing infection.

questionText: Which one of the following is not a true statement about Chlamydi
options: a. Requires tissue culture for growth
Has the nuclear structure of a virus
explanation: Chlamydia is a true bacterium, not a virus, and therefore does not have the nuclear structure of a virus. Chlamydia requires an intracellular environment to replicate, but it is not a virus. Chlamydia's nuclear structure is typical of bacteria, with a single circular chromosome.

questionText: Which of the following species are gram positive:
explanation: Listeria species are gram-positive, rod-shaped bacteria that can cause listeriosis. They exhibit a characteristic gram-positive staining pattern with a thick peptidoglycan cell wall. This is in contrast to gram-negative bacteria, which have a thinner peptidoglycan layer and an outer lipid bilayer.

questionText: Which of the following media is commonly used when performing the Kirby-Bauer disk diffusion
explanation: Mueller-Hinton agar is the preferred medium for the Kirby-Bauer disk diffusion test because it has a low nutrient content, allowing for consistent growth of bacteria and accurate measurement of antibiotic susceptibility.

questionText: Which of the following best defines "sensitivity":
options: The percentage of patients with a disease who will have a positive test
The percentage of patients without a disease who will have a negative test
The percentage of patients with a disease who will have a negative test

The percentage of patients without a disease who will have a positive test Feedback: Sensitivity refers to the percentage or fraction of patients with a given disease in a givenpopulation who will have a positive test.
explanation: Sensitivity is a measure of a test's ability to correctly identify those with the disease, calculated as the number of true positives divided by the sum of true positives and false negatives.

questionText: What percentage solution of sodium hypochlorite (bleach) is recommended as a routine laboratory disinfectant:
explanation: A 10% solution of sodium hypochlorite is recommended as a routine laboratory disinfectant because it provides a balance between efficacy and safety, effectively killing a wide range of microorganisms while minimizing the risk of damage to equipment and surfaces.

questionText: In HDN which of the following antigen-antibody reactions is occurring:
explanation: In Hemolytic Disease of the Newborn (HDN), the maternal immune system produces antibodies against the antigens present on the red blood cells of the fetus, leading to hemolysis. This is an example of an antibody-mediated reaction, where the maternal antibody reacts against the fetal antigen. This reaction is the primary cause of the disease.

questionText: Carbon dioxide is predominately found in blood in the form of:
explanation: Carbon dioxide is predominately found in blood in the form of bicarbonate ions (HCO3-) due to the action of the enzyme carbonic anhydrase, which catalyzes the reversible reaction of carbon dioxide and water to form carbonic acid, which then dissociates into hydrogen ions and bicarbonate ions. This process occurs in red blood cells and is essential for maintaining acid-base balance in the body. Bicarbonate ions are the primary form of CO2 transport in the blood.

questionText: In a normal CSF the protein concentration as compared to that in the serum is generally:
options: Less than 1% Feedback: Normal ratio of serum to CSF Protein is about 200 to 1, or less than 1%. Elevation of CSF total protein is a nonspecific finding, but usually indicates some type of disease involving the brain or meninges.
explanation: The normal ratio of serum to CSF protein is about 200 to 1, indicating that the protein concentration in CSF is less than 1% of that in serum. This is a fundamental principle in clinical laboratory medicine, and any significant deviation from this ratio can indicate underlying neurological conditions.

questionText: Which of the following staining methods would you use to demonstrate the metachromatic granules of Corynebacterium diphtheriae:
options: Methyleneblue Feedback: Methylene blue stain can be used to visualize the metachromatic granules that are characteristic of C. diphtheriae.
explanation: Methylene blue stain is used to visualize the metachromatic granules of Corynebacterium diphtheriae due to its ability to bind to the granules, making them visible under a microscope. This staining method is particularly useful for identifying C. diphtheriae in clinical specimens. The metachromatic granules are a key characteristic of this bacterium.

questionText: Which of the following are not considered normal flora of the gastrointestinal tract:
options: Shigella Feedback: Shigella and Salmonella are not found as normal flora in the gastrointestinal tract.
explanation: Shigella and Salmonella are not considered normal flora of the gastrointestinal tract because they are pathogenic bacteria that can cause disease in humans. They are typically associated with gastrointestinal infections, whereas normal flora are typically commensal organisms that do not cause disease. In this context, Peptostreptococcus is a normal flora of the gastrointestinal tract.

questionText: All of the following cellular antigens are important to an immunohematologist except:
options: Autoantigens Feedback: A hapten is an incomplete antigen.
explanation: Haptens are small molecules that require a carrier protein to become immunogenic, and are not typically considered cellular antigens. Immunohematologists focus on the interaction between the immune system and blood cells, making haptens less relevant to their field. In contrast, blood group antigens, histocompatibility antigens, and autoantigens are all important in immunohematology.

questionText: Which one of the following statements about anti-A1 is false:
options: Anti-A1 is a naturally occurring antibody that is usually clinically insignificant
Anti-A1 reactive at 37oC can sometimes destroy transfused A1 positive cells
A1 and A2 occur in 80 and 20 percent of the population, respectively
A2 cells react with Dolichos biflorus lectin Feedback: Dolichos biflorus lectin has anti-A1 specificity.
explanation: A1 and A2 blood types occur in approximately 6% and 96% of the population, respectively, not 80 and 20 percent as stated in option C. This discrepancy makes option C the false statement.

questionText: Which one of the following organisms do not usually stain with an acid-fast stain, or one of its variants:
explanation: Cryptosporidium does not stain with acid-fast stain because it is a protozoan parasite, whereas the other options are bacteria that typically exhibit acid-fast properties due to their cell wall composition.

questionText: Which of the following would be the most appropriate temperature for long term storage of viral cultures:
options: Room temperature Feedback: Cultures can be stored at either -20° or -70°, but -70° is preferred for long term storage.
explanation: Viral cultures are typically stored at -70°C for long-term preservation due to its ability to maintain viability and prevent degradation of the viral genome, ensuring accurate results when the cultures are thawed and used for further testing or research.

questionText: Which of the following would be the most appropriate method to confirm a positive protein from a urine dipstick: Immunoelectropheresis
explanation: Sulfosalicylic acid precipitation is a simple and effective method to confirm the presence of protein in urine, as it can detect even small amounts of protein. This method is commonly used in clinical laboratories due to its ease of use and rapid results. It is a suitable confirmatory test for a positive protein result from a urine dipstick.

questionText: Circulating organic iodine is found primarily in the form of:
options: Thyroxine Feedback: Iodine circulates as thyroxine (T4) and to and to a lesser extent as Triiodothyronine (T3).
explanation: Circulating organic iodine is primarily found as thyroxine (T4), which is a hormone produced by the thyroid gland. Thyroxine is the main form of iodine in the blood, and it is converted to triiodothyronine (T3) in peripheral tissues. This conversion is necessary for T3 to exert its biological effects.

questionText: Which of the following conditions would be suggested by a marked rise in alkalinephosphatase, jaundice, and a moderate rise in ALT:
options: Renal failure Feedback: Post-hepatic obstruction is characterized by a marked increase in conjugated bilirubin.
explanation: A marked rise in alkaline phosphatase and jaundice, along with a moderate rise in ALT, suggests post-hepatic obstruction. This is because alkaline phosphatase is elevated in conditions involving bile duct obstruction, and jaundice indicates elevated bilirubin levels. The moderate rise in ALT also supports this diagnosis, as it indicates some degree of hepatocellular injury.

questionText: Which of the following organisms is the most common cause of acute cystitis:
explanation: Escherichia coli is the most common cause of acute cystitis due to its prevalence in the human gut and its ability to adhere to and colonize the bladder mucosa, leading to urinary tract infections.

questionText: A fluorometer operates on which of the following principles:
options: Measures amount of light absorbed by a given compound
Measures changes in emitted wavelength of light after absorption by an analyte
Measures amount of light scattered by the analyte in question
Measures light emitted at two or more wavelengths
explanation: A fluorometer operates on the principle of measuring the amount of light emitted by a fluorescent compound after it has absorbed light of a specific wavelength. This is based on the principle of fluorescence, where the analyte absorbs light at one wavelength and emits light at another wavelength. This principle is commonly used in clinical laboratory medicine for the quantification of various analytes, such as bilirubin and thyroxine.

questionText: Which of the following statement about synovial fluid is true:
options: Markedly elevated neutrophils always correspond to bacterial joint infection
Patients with gout involving joints will have markedly elevated neutrophils in their synovial fluid
Fungal joint infections have synovial fluid with numerous lymphocytes
Tuberculous joint infections have synovial fluid with numerous plasma cells
explanation: Markedly elevated neutrophils in synovial fluid are characteristic of bacterial joint infections, as neutrophils are a type of white blood cell that responds to bacterial infections. In bacterial joint infections, the neutrophil count in synovial fluid can be significantly elevated, often exceeding 25,000 cells per microliter. This is a key diagnostic feature that distinguishes bacterial joint infections from other types of joint inflammation.

questionText: Rheumatoid factor reacts with which the following :
explanation: Rheumatoid factor is an autoantibody that reacts with the Fc fragment of IgG, which is a component of the immune complex found in rheumatoid arthritis. This reaction is a hallmark of the disease and is used as a diagnostic marker. The Fc fragment is the crystallizable fragment of an antibody that interacts with Fc receptors and some proteins that bind to the Fc region.

questionText: Gamma irradiation of cellular blood components is required in which of the following situations:
options: Prevent non-cardiogenic pulmonaryedema Feedback: Transfusion related Graft-Versus-Host disease is a rare condition usually following transfusion of patients whose immune system is severely compromised. It occurs when T lymphocytes present in the transfused unit replicate and attack the tissues of the recipient. Gamma irradiation prevents this condition by inactivating T lymphocytes in the donor unit. Gamma irradiation of cellular blood components is required when: 1.The donor is a blood relative of the recipient,
explanation: Gamma irradiation prevents Graft-Versus-Host disease by inactivating T lymphocytes in the donor unit, which would otherwise replicate and attack the recipient's tissues.

questionText: Patients with which of the following conditions would benefit most from washed red cells:
options: Multiple red cell alloantibodies Feedback: Washing not only reduces the number of leukocytes and platelets that are often responsible for febrile reactions, but also eliminates anticoagulants, ammonia, lactic acid, and potassium.
explanation: Washed red cells are beneficial for patients with warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia because the washing process removes leukocytes and platelets that can exacerbate the condition, as well as anticoagulants and other substances that can cause adverse reactions.

questionText: Cryoglobulin testing can be used to:
options: Help diagnose Raynaud's syndrome Feedback: Cryoglobulin is an abnormal serum protein with a unique ability to precipitate when exposed to cold temperatures. Cryoglobulin is present in Raynaud's syndrome.
explanation: Cryoglobulin testing is used to help diagnose Raynaud's syndrome because cryoglobulins are abnormal serum proteins that precipitate in cold temperatures, which is a characteristic feature of this condition. The presence of cryoglobulins in the blood can indicate an underlying autoimmune disorder, such as Raynaud's syndrome. This test is particularly useful in cases where the clinical presentation is suggestive of Raynaud's syndrome.

questionText: Which is arranged from least mature to most mature:
options: Myeloblast, Myelocyte, Band, Neutrophil, Metamyelocyte, Promyelocyte, Stem Cell
Stem Cell, Myeloblast, Promyelocyte, Myelocyte, Metamyelocyte, Band, Neutrophil
Stem Cell, Promyelocyte, Metamyelocyte, Neutrophil, Myeloblast, Myelocyte,Band
Neutrophil, Band, Metamyelocyte, Myelocyte, Promyelocyte, Myeloblast, StemCell
explanation: The correct sequence is based on the maturation stages of neutrophils in the bone marrow, starting from the least mature (Stem Cell) to the most mature (Neutrophil). This sequence is essential for understanding the development and function of neutrophils in the body. The correct sequence reflects the normal process of neutrophil maturation.

questionText: The measurement of total glycosylated hemoglobin A1c is an effective means of assessing the average blood glucose levels:
options: Only the past 24 hours Feedback: The concentration of hemoglobin A1c is directly proportional to the average plasma glucose level that the RBCs are exposed to during their 120 day life span. The glycosylated hemoglobin result from glycosylation of serine, asparagine, and hydroxylysine residues in hemoglobin. There are three glycosylated hemoglobins: Hb A1a, Hb A1b, and Hb A1c, of which Hb A1c constitutes 80%. Most methods measure total gycosylated hemoglobin, which has a high degree of correlation to Hb A1c, and may be reported as such after making the appropriate conversion.
explanation: The measurement of total glycosylated hemoglobin A1c is an effective means of assessing the average blood glucose levels over the past 2-3 months because it reflects the concentration of hemoglobin A1c, which is directly proportional to the average plasma glucose level that the RBCs are exposed to during their 120-day life span.

questionText: Bacitracin susceptibility is useful for which two of the following:
options: Presumptive identification of Group A streptococci

Identification of Neisseria Feedback: Staphylococci are resistant to bacitracin while micrococcus are sensitive. Group A beta-hemolytic Streptococci are sensitive to bacitracin, while most other Groups are resistant.
explanation: Bacitracin susceptibility is useful for distinguishing Staphylococci from micrococci because Staphylococci are resistant to bacitracin, while micrococcus are sensitive. This is a key characteristic used in clinical laboratory medicine to differentiate between these two types of bacteria. The sensitivity of micrococci to bacitracin is a useful diagnostic tool.

questionText: Which of the following is the proper temperature to use when crossmatching in the presence of a cold antibody:
options: 4 degrees Celsius Feedback: Most antibodies that are inactive at 37 degrees Celsius, and active only below 37 degreesCelsius (i.e. cold reactive antibodies), are of little clinical significance.
explanation: Cold antibodies are typically IgM antibodies that are active at temperatures below 37 degrees Celsius. Performing crossmatching at a lower temperature (e.g. 15 degrees Celsius) can help to identify these antibodies, which may be clinically significant in certain situations such as transfusion reactions.

questionText: When a urine specimen cannot be cultured immediately it may be:
options: Stored at room temperature for up to 8hours
Stored in freezer for up to 24 hours
Stored at 4° C for up to 24 hours
explanation: Neisseria is a type of bacteria that requires a specific type of media for growth, which is typically not available in a standard clinical laboratory setting. Therefore, it is not a viable option for a urine specimen that cannot be cultured immediately. The correct options for storing a urine specimen are to store it at room temperature for up to 8 hours or at 4°C for up to 24 hours.

questionText: Platelet should be stored at what temperature :
options: 34-37 degreesCelsius Feedback: Platelets should be stored at 20-24 degrees Celsius with continuous gentle agitation. They should be infused within 4 hours after the seal on a platelet unit is broken.
explanation: Platelets should be stored at 20-24 degrees Celsius to maintain their viability and function, as temperatures outside this range can lead to activation and aggregation of platelets, affecting their transfusion efficacy.

questionText: The recommended temperature/time/pressure for routine steam sterilization of media is:
explanation: The recommended temperature/time/pressure for routine steam sterilization of media is 121°C for 12-15 minutes at 15 psi, as this temperature and time combination is sufficient to kill all forms of microbial life, including spores, which are the most resistant to heat.

questionText: Which of the following casts might be found in the urine of a healthy individual after strenuous exercise:
options: Waxy casts Feedback: Hyaline casts may be seen in healthy individuals particularly after exercise.
explanation: Hyaline casts are normal findings in urine, particularly after strenuous exercise, as they are formed from the concentration of Tamm-Horsfall mucoprotein in the renal tubules. They are not indicative of kidney damage or disease. Their presence in a healthy individual after exercise is a benign finding.

questionText: If a laboratory 's control range (using a 99.7 confidence interval) for a given assay is 20.0 to50.0, what would it’s means and one standard deviation be:
options: Mean = 35.0 SD =5.0 Feedback: The mean would be halfway between 20 and 50, or
explanation: The control range is a 99.7% confidence interval, which corresponds to 3 standard deviations from the mean in a normal distribution. Since the range is 20.0 to 50.0, the mean would be halfway between 20 and 50, which is 35.0. The one standard deviation would be 1/3 of the range, which is (50.0-20.0)/6 = 5.0.

questionText: If a potential donor has been transfused blood products, he must be deferred from blood donation for:
explanation: A potential donor who has been transfused blood products must be deferred from blood donation for 6 months due to the risk of transmitting infectious agents such as hepatitis B and C, and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). This deferral period allows for the window period of these infections to pass, ensuring the safety of the blood supply. The exact deferral period may vary depending on the specific circumstances and local regulations.

questionText: An urticarial reaction is characterized by:
options: Blood in the urine Feedback: Urticarial transfusion reactions occur in up to 1% of transfusions. They are manifested by hives, rash, and itching. The transfusion may be resumed after successful administration of antihistamines.
explanation: An urticarial reaction is characterized by a rash and hives, which are manifestations of an allergic response. This reaction is often seen in transfusion reactions and can be managed with antihistamines. The presence of hives and rash distinguishes urticarial reactions from other types of transfusion reactions.

questionText: Which of the following cells when found upon microscopic examination of the urine would be most indicative of kidney disease:
options: RBCs Feedback: Squamous epithelial cells are usually vaginal contaminants.
explanation: The presence of squamous epithelial cells in the urine is often indicative of contamination, but in the context of kidney disease, it can also suggest a fistula or abnormal connection between the urinary and vaginal systems, allowing vaginal cells to enter the urine. However, the most common and direct indicator of kidney disease is the presence of red blood cells (RBCs) in the urine, which can be seen in conditions such as glomerulonephritis or kidney stones. RBCs are not listed as an option, but it's worth noting that they would be the most indicative of kidney disease.

questionText: Which of the following statistical methods would be employed to determine how closely two different methods compare with each other:
options: Percent difference of means Feedback: Linear regression can be used to compare one method with another.
explanation: Linear regression is used to evaluate the relationship between two variables, making it suitable for comparing the performance of two different methods. This statistical method can help identify if there is a significant correlation between the results obtained from each method, allowing for a more accurate assessment of their agreement. In clinical laboratory medicine, linear regression is often employed to validate new testing methods against established ones.

questionText: Elevation in CSF total protein may be seen in all of the following conditions except:
explanation: Parkinson's disease is a neurodegenerative disorder primarily affecting movement, and it does not typically cause an elevation in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) total protein. Elevated CSF total protein is often seen in conditions that cause inflammation or damage to the central nervous system, such as bacterial meningitis, brain tumors, and cerebrovascular accidents (CVAs).

questionText: Which one of the following is not a system for incubation of anaerobic bacteri
explanation: The Candle jar is not a suitable system for incubation of anaerobic bacteria as it relies on the combustion of a candle to consume oxygen, which is not a reliable or controlled method for maintaining anaerobic conditions.

questionText: A plastic anemia may be caused by all of the following except:
options: Ionizing radiation Feedback: Enzyme deficiencies are usually associated with hemolytic anemias.
explanation: Enzyme deficiencies are typically associated with disorders that cause hemolysis, such as glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, rather than aplastic anemia. Aplastic anemia is characterized by bone marrow failure to produce blood cells, which is not directly related to enzyme deficiencies. This condition is more commonly caused by infections, chemical agents, or ionizing radiation.

questionText: Which of the following types of whole blood would be the least satisfactory to transfuse to a type AB patient:
options: GroupAB Feedback: Group O whole blood contains both anti-A and anti-B which could react with the recipient'sRBCs.
explanation: Group O whole blood contains both anti-A and anti-B antibodies, which could react with the recipient's red blood cells, causing a hemolytic transfusion reaction in a type AB patient.

questionText: Bence-Jones proteinuria is associated with all of the following conditions except:
options: Amyloidosis Feedback: Macroglobulinemia, Multiple Myeloma, and Amyloidosis are all associated with abnormal protein production and/or accumulation which can result in Bence-Jones proteins being excreted in the urine.
explanation: Pernicious anemia is a condition characterized by a deficiency in vitamin B12, which is not directly associated with abnormal protein production or Bence-Jones proteinuria. Bence-Jones proteins are typically associated with plasma cell dyscrasias, such as multiple myeloma and macroglobulinemia, or conditions involving abnormal protein accumulation, like amyloidosis.

questionText: The slide coagulase test is a rapid method for identifying which of the following organisms.
options: Neisseria gonorrhoeae Feedback: Since not all isolates of S. aureus are detected by the slide coagulase test, suspicious organisms negative by the slide test must be confirmed by the tube coagulase test.
explanation: The slide coagulase test is a rapid method for identifying Staphylococcus aureus, as it detects the coagulase enzyme produced by this organism. However, not all isolates of S. aureus are detected by the slide test, which is why suspicious organisms must be confirmed by the tube coagulase test. This test is essential for distinguishing S. aureus from other Staphylococcus species.

questionText: Which of the following streptococcus exhibits a positive bile solubility test:
options: S. mutans Feedback: Streptococcus pneumoniae colonies dissolve with the addition of sodium deoxycholate (positive bile sensitivity test) and are sensitive to Optochin- unlike other species of Streptococci.
explanation: Streptococcus pneumoniae exhibits a positive bile solubility test due to its colonies dissolving with the addition of sodium deoxycholate, a characteristic used to differentiate it from other Streptococci species.

questionText: Which of the following red blood cells contain the most H antigen:
options: Bombayphenotype Feedback: O cells contain only H antigen, while cells of the other ABO groups contain varying amount of H antigen in addition to their group specific antigen(s). The classic Bombay phenotype is characterized by the absence of A, B, and H antigens.
explanation: The Bombay phenotype, characterized by the absence of A, B, and H antigens, contains only H antigen on its red blood cells. This is because the H antigen is the precursor to A and B antigens, and its presence is necessary for the expression of A and B antigens. Therefore, the Bombay phenotype contains the most H antigen.

questionText: A zinc deficiency in the elderly is often caused by:
explanation: Zinc deficiency in the elderly is often caused by decreased intake and absorption due to inadequate dietary zinc, impaired zinc absorption from the gastrointestinal tract, and increased zinc excretion, which can be exacerbated by age-related changes in the body.

questionText: ABO blood groups were discovered by:
options: Landsteiner Feedback: Landsteiner first identified the presence of the separate red cell antigens A and B in the early1900's.
explanation: Landsteiner first identified the presence of the separate red cell antigens A and B in the early 1900's, marking a significant milestone in the understanding of ABO blood groups.

questionText: Which of the following parasites is not commonly found in the peripheral blood:
options: Onchocerca volvulus Feedback: The microfiliariae of Onchocerca do not generally circulate in the peripheral blood. The diagnosis is made by demonstrating the microfiliariae in teased skin snips.
explanation: Onchocerca volvulus microfilariae are not typically found in peripheral blood, making skin snips a necessary diagnostic tool. This is in contrast to other filarial parasites, such as Loa loa, Brugia malayi, and Dipetalonema perstans, which can be detected in peripheral blood. The absence of Onchocerca volvulus microfilariae in peripheral blood is a key distinguishing feature of this parasite.

questionText: If an Rh negative patient is administered a unit of R1R1 packed red cells, which one of the following antibodies would be most likely to develop:
options: Anti-e Feedback: R1R1 (DCe/DCe) cells are positive for the D antigen, which is the most immunogenic antigen of the Rh system, followed by c and E.
explanation: The D antigen is the most immunogenic antigen of the Rh system, making it the most likely to induce an immune response in an Rh negative patient. This patient would be at risk of developing anti-D antibodies after receiving R1R1 packed red cells, which express the D antigen. This reaction can lead to hemolysis and other complications in future transfusions.

questionText: A decrease in which of the following in AIDS patients results in increased susceptibility to infection:
options: HIV antigens Feedback: It is the CD 4+ cells that help aid our immune system in attacking foreign antigens by initiating the body's response. CD 8+ also helps in the role of immunity by attaching to infected cells to initiate cell destruction. A decrease in HIV antibodies would not leave the host more susceptible to infection since the antibody is directed at the HIV virus only. Finally, a decrease in HIV antigens will also not cause a host to become more suseptible to infections.
explanation: A decrease in CD4+ cells compromises the immune system's ability to initiate an effective response against foreign antigens, increasing susceptibility to infection in AIDS patients.

questionText: The primary site of reabsorption of glomerular filtrate is the:
explanation: The primary site of reabsorption of glomerular filtrate is the proximal convoluted tubule, where approximately 70-80% of the filtered glucose, amino acids, and other nutrients are reabsorbed back into the bloodstream.

questionText: Which of these is arranged from least mature to most mature:
explanation: The correct sequence from least mature to most mature is Stem Cell, Lymphoblast, Lymphocyte, and then Prolymphocyte. This sequence reflects the developmental progression of lymphoid cells, with stem cells giving rise to lymphoblasts, which then mature into lymphocytes and in some cases, prolymphocytes. This sequence is a fundamental concept in clinical laboratory medicine.

questionText: MCV is calculated using which of the following parameters:
options: RBC and MCHC Feedback: MCV = Hematocrit X 1000/RBC (in millions per microliter). The MCV is expressed in femtoliters (cubic micrometers, 10-15 liters).
explanation: MCV is calculated by dividing the hematocrit (Hct) by the RBC count, then multiplying by 10^(-12) or 1000, which is equivalent to femtoliters. This formula is MCV = Hct x 1000/RBC. The correct answer reflects this calculation.

questionText: Which of the following would not be considered a normal part of a routine electrolyte panel:
options: Chloride Feedback: A routine electrolyte panel typically consists of sodium, potassium, chloride, bicarbonate, creatinine, glucose, and BUN.
explanation: Magnesium is not typically included in a routine electrolyte panel, which usually consists of sodium, potassium, chloride, bicarbonate, creatinine, glucose, and BUN. Magnesium is often measured as part of a comprehensive metabolic panel or in specific clinical scenarios. Its exclusion is due to its relatively narrow therapeutic range and the fact that it is not as commonly monitored as other electrolytes.

questionText: Which of the following conditions is associated with elevated serum uric acid levels:
options: Gout Feedback: Gout is a disease manifested by the deposition of crystalline uric acid in joints and soft tissues,with secondary inflammation and pain.
explanation: Elevated serum uric acid levels are characteristic of gout, as the body's inability to properly excrete uric acid leads to its deposition in joints and soft tissues, causing inflammation and pain.

questionText: Which of the following additives should be used for the collection of a sample for blood gas analysis:
explanation: Sodium oxalate is used as an anticoagulant for blood gas analysis because it effectively chelates calcium ions, preventing clotting and ensuring accurate results.

questionText: What is the site used most frequently in the adult patient when performing a bone marrow biopsy:
options: Iliac crest Feedback: Bone marrow specimens are usually obtained in adults from the posterior iliac crest. They may also be obtained from the sternum.
explanation: The posterior iliac crest is the preferred site for bone marrow biopsy in adults due to its accessibility and the high concentration of bone marrow in this area, allowing for a more accurate and representative sample.

questionText: The precursor of the platelet which is commonly only found in the bone marrow is:
options: Erythroblast Feedback: Platelets are formed by the fragmentation of megakaryocyte cytoplasm.
explanation: The megakaryocyte is the precursor cell to platelets, and it is primarily found in the bone marrow. As it matures, it undergoes fragmentation, releasing platelets into the circulation. This process is essential for maintaining normal platelet counts and function.

questionText: Which of the following set of conditions would preclude HDN as a result of Rh incompatibility:
options: Mother Rh unknown, baby Rh-positive Feedback: If both parents are Rh negative, the baby would also be Rh negative.
explanation: If both parents are Rh negative, the baby would also be Rh negative, eliminating the risk of hemolytic disease of the newborn (HDN) due to Rh incompatibility. This is because Rh negative individuals can only produce antibodies against Rh positive blood, and if the baby is also Rh negative, there will be no Rh positive blood for the mother's immune system to react against. As a result, there will be no hemolysis of the baby's red blood cells.

questionText: Erythropoietin is produced in:
options: Kidneys Feedback: Erythropoietin, which is produced in the kidneys, stimulates the production of red blood cells.
explanation: Erythropoietin is a hormone that stimulates red blood cell production, and it is primarily produced in the kidneys in response to low oxygen levels in the blood. The kidneys produce erythropoietin in response to hypoxia, which then stimulates the bone marrow to produce more red blood cells. This process is essential for maintaining adequate oxygen delivery to tissues and organs.

questionText: The Rh nomenclature which uses the letters DCE is found in which of the following genetic models:
options: Rhesus Feedback: Fisher and Race first proposed the existence of the three closely linked genes, and used the DCE terminology to describe their theory.
explanation: The Fisher-Race model uses the DCE terminology to describe the three closely linked genes, making it the correct answer. This model was proposed by Fisher and Race to explain the Rh blood group system. The DCE terminology represents the three genes that control the Rh blood group antigens.

questionText: Which of the following organisms is an obligate intracellular parasite:
explanation: Rickettsiae are obligate intracellular parasites, meaning they require a host cell to replicate and survive. They are typically transmitted through the bites of infected ticks or fleas and can cause diseases such as typhus and spotted fever. In the clinical laboratory, Rickettsiae are often detected through serological tests or PCR.

questionText: An average adult would excrete approximately what volume of urine per 24 hours:
options: 250 ml Feedback: Normal adult urine volume is 800 to 1800 ml/24hours for males, and 600 to 1600 ml/24 hours for females.
explanation: The normal adult urine volume ranges from 800 to 1800 ml/24 hours for males and 600 to 1600 ml/24 hours for females, making 1500ml a suitable average value.

questionText: What minimum level of specific resistance (megohms@25oC) is required for a Type I watersystem:
options: 0.1 Feedback: Specific resistance is the resistance in Ohms of a 1 cm long by 1 cm2 cross sectional column of solution. Type I water is the purest, and therefore has the highest resistance. Type II water is used for most routine laboratory determinations, and must have a specific resistance of at least 2.
explanation: Type I water is the purest and has the highest specific resistance, typically requiring a minimum of 10.0 megohms at 25°C to ensure optimal laboratory results and prevent contamination.

questionText: Which of the following group B antigens is generally associated with a mixed field reaction:
options: Bx Feedback: B3 is characterized by a weaker than usual reaction with anti-B and by a mixed field reaction with the same reagent.
explanation: Group B3 antigens are characterized by a weaker reaction with anti-B reagents and a mixed field reaction, which is a result of the partial expression of the B antigen. This mixed field reaction is due to the incomplete expression of the B antigen, leading to a combination of both B and non-B reactions. This phenomenon is a key feature of group B3 antigens in clinical laboratory medicine.

questionText: The most common rapid slide test (MONOSPOTâ) for infectious mononucleosis employs:
options: None of the above Feedback: A positive spot test shows agglutination of horse erythrocytes when added to patient serum previously absorbed with guinea pig kidney, but not when added to patient serum previously absorbed with beef erythrocyte stroma. The test is generally simple, sensitive, and specific, but false negative are common in young children with mononucleosis.
explanation: The MONOSPOT test employs horse erythrocytes due to the specific agglutination reaction that occurs when patient serum, previously absorbed with guinea pig kidney, is added to the horse erythrocytes. This reaction is indicative of infectious mononucleosis. The use of horse erythrocytes allows for the differentiation between specific and non-specific agglutination reactions.

questionText: Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is associated with all of the following clinical conditions except:
options: Thrombocytosis Feedback: Platelet counts are decreased or normal during DIC.
explanation: Intravascular hemolysis is not a direct cause of DIC, although it can be a consequence of DIC. DIC is characterized by the consumption of platelets and coagulation factors, leading to a decrease in platelet counts, not thrombocytosis.

questionText: Which of the following organisms is most likely to be associated with gas gangrene:
explanation: Clostridium perfringens is a gram-positive, anaerobic bacterium that produces toxins causing gas gangrene, a severe and potentially life-threatening condition characterized by tissue necrosis and gas production in the affected area.

questionText: Which of the following would most likely occur as the result of hemodilution:
options: Electrolyte concentrations would remain the same Feedback: A dilutional effect caused by the sample being hemodiluted, would not cause high serum electrolytes since they have been diluted out. The anion gap could remain the same or become decreased. Finally, the electrolyte concentrations could not remain the same, since there will be a smaller amount in the sample to test due to the diluent.
explanation: Hemodilution occurs when a sample is diluted with a solution, resulting in a decrease in the concentration of serum electrolytes. This is because the diluent contains electrolytes that are added to the sample, causing the electrolyte concentration to decrease. As a result, the serum electrolyte levels will be lower than normal.

questionText: Following a myocardial infarction which of the following enzymes will be the first to become elevated:
options: AST Feedback: GGT is elevated in liver disorders. CK rises before LDH. However myoglobin is the earliest serum cardiac marker to rise after an infarction; it may be positive within two hours post MI. It is not cardiac specific, and can be elevated in skeletal muscle trauma or rhabdomyolysis.
explanation: Myoglobin is the earliest serum cardiac marker to rise after a myocardial infarction, often becoming positive within two hours post-MI. It is not cardiac specific, as it can be elevated in skeletal muscle trauma or rhabdomyolysis. However, in the context of the provided options, myoglobin is implied as the correct answer, making CK the next earliest enzyme to become elevated.

questionText: India Ink is used to:
options: Visualize cytoplasm Feedback: India ink can aid in the visualization of the polysacchride capsules of yeast such as Cryptococcus neoformans.
explanation: India ink is used to visualize the polysaccharide capsule of yeast such as Cryptococcus neoformans, which appears as a halo around the yeast cells due to the negative staining technique.

questionText: The most frequent genotype among Rho(D) -negative persons is:
explanation: The most frequent genotype among Rho(D)-negative persons is 'rr' because it represents the homozygous recessive genotype, where an individual inherits two copies of the RHD gene variant that leads to Rho(D) negativity.

questionText: Which one tests should be used to monitor a patient's response to treatment for syphilis:
options: TPHA titer Feedback: RPR titer should be performed every three months for one year; a fourfold increase in titer indicates infection, reinfection, or failed treatment; a fourfold decrease in titer indicates adequate treatment.
explanation: The RPR (Rapid Plasma Reagin) titer is used to monitor a patient's response to treatment for syphilis because it measures the level of antibodies against the syphilis bacterium. A fourfold decrease in RPR titer indicates adequate treatment, while a fourfold increase suggests infection, reinfection, or failed treatment. This makes RPR titer a crucial test for assessing treatment efficacy.

questionText: Which of the following anticoagulants will not produce a significant effect on calcium levels in plasm
options: Citrates Feedback: EDTA, Oxalates, and Citrates remove calcium from the blood, while heparin acts by forming a complex with antithrombin III.
explanation: Heparin acts by forming a complex with antithrombin III, which activates the coagulation pathway, and does not directly remove calcium from the blood like EDTA, oxalates, and citrates. This makes heparin the correct answer as it does not significantly affect calcium levels in plasma.

questionText: Which of the following kappa / lambda ratios is found in normal serum:
explanation: The normal kappa/lambda ratio in serum is typically around 1:1, as both kappa and lambda light chains are produced in equal amounts by plasma cells. A ratio of 2:1 or higher may indicate a monoclonal gammopathy, such as multiple myeloma. This is because a single clone of plasma cells produces excess kappa or lambda light chains.

questionText: The A1 subgroup represents approximately what percentage of group A individuals:
options: 95% Feedback: Approximately 80% of all people typed as group A or AB are agglutinated by anti- A1 sera.
explanation: The A1 subgroup is a subset of individuals with group A blood type, and approximately 80% of those with group A or AB blood types are agglutinated by anti-A1 sera, indicating the prevalence of the A1 antigen in this population.

questionText: The infective stage for all of the intestinal amoebae is the:
options: Egg Feedback: The majority of the amoebae pass through two life cycle stages: a delicate feeding stage call a trophozoite, and a non-feeding infective cyst. Recovery of either form is considered diagnostic.
explanation: The infective stage for intestinal amoebae is the cyst, as it is the non-feeding form that can survive outside the host and transmit the infection. The cyst stage is resistant to environmental stress and can be ingested by a new host, allowing the infection to continue. This is in contrast to the trophozoite stage, which is the feeding form that causes disease but is not infective.

questionText: Which of the following is false about troponin:
options: It rises much sooner after an MI than CK-MB
It stays positive much longer than CK-MB
It is potentially more specific than CK-MB

Troponin T is often elevated in renal failure patients Feedback: Troponin is potentially more specific for myocardial damage than CK-MB and stays elevated longer. It may eventually replace CK-MB as the standard marker of myocardial damage. Troponin and CK-MB both tend to rise approximately 3 hours after a MI; however, troponins can stay elevated up to 2 weeks as CK-MB tends to return to baseline around 36 hours.
explanation: Troponin does not stay positive much longer than CK-MB, as both tend to rise approximately 3 hours after a myocardial infarction (MI) and troponin can stay elevated up to 2 weeks, while CK-MB tends to return to baseline around 36 hours.

questionText: What is the purpose of using methyl alcohol in the gram stain procedure:
options: Fix all gram negative organisms Feedback: Gram positive organisms resist decolorization by methyl alcohol.
explanation: Gram positive organisms resist decolorization by methyl alcohol due to the presence of a thick peptidoglycan layer in their cell walls, which prevents the solvent from penetrating and removing the crystal violet stain. This results in the characteristic purple color of gram positive bacteria. Methyl alcohol is used to decolorize gram negative organisms, which have a thinner peptidoglycan layer and are more susceptible to decolorization.

questionText: Nephelometry involves the measurement:
options: Atomic absorption Feedback: Nephelometry is used to measure the light scattered by particles in a solution. It is useful for measuring protein levels in fluids, and antigen-antibody complexes.
explanation: Nephelometry measures the light scattered by particles in a solution, making it useful for detecting and quantifying protein levels and antigen-antibody complexes in fluids. This technique is particularly useful in clinical laboratory medicine for diagnosing and monitoring various conditions, such as kidney disease and autoimmune disorders.

questionText: Which of the following procedures would you employ to monitor the precision of an assay:
options: Run samples in duplicate Feedback: Precision is a measure of reproducibility of a test when it is repeated several times under the same conditions. It could be monitored by running samples in duplicate or triplicate.
explanation: Precision in clinical laboratory medicine is evaluated by assessing the reproducibility of a test when it is repeated under the same conditions. Running blinded samples in duplicate or triplicate allows for the calculation of coefficients of variation, which is a key indicator of precision. This method helps to identify any systematic errors or biases in the assay.

questionText: Which of the following immunoglobulin classes is chiefly responsible for the degranulation of mast cells and basophils:
options: IgE Feedback: IgE levels are often increased in patients with allergic disease. IgE binds to the membranes of mast cells and basophils, and if specific antigen is present to react with the IgE molecule, degranulation of these cells occurs, releasing histamines, and other substances into the blood or tissues.
explanation: IgE is the primary immunoglobulin responsible for triggering the degranulation of mast cells and basophils, leading to the release of histamine and other mediators involved in allergic reactions.

questionText: The lecethin to sphingomyelin ratio (L/S) is used to assess:
options: Fetal liver development Feedback: An L/S ratio above 2:1 indicates mature lung development, whereas a ratio below 1.5:1indicates pulmonary immaturity.
explanation: The lecithin to sphingomyelin ratio (L/S) is a test used to assess fetal lung maturity. An L/S ratio above 2:1 indicates mature lung development, whereas a ratio below 1.5:1 indicates pulmonary immaturity. This is crucial for determining the optimal time for delivery in preterm infants.

questionText: What additional fraction would be seen if plasma rather than serum was subjected to electrophoresis:
options: Fibrinogen Feedback: Fibrinogen present in plasma would form a band between the beta and gamma globulins.
explanation: Fibrinogen is a large glycoprotein that is present in plasma but coagulates upon clotting to form fibrin. When plasma is subjected to electrophoresis, fibrinogen migrates more slowly than the beta globulins, forming a distinct band between them.

questionText: Which of the following is a routine staining technique used in the clinical laboratory:
explanation: Romanowsky staining is a routine staining technique used in the clinical laboratory for the differential diagnosis of blood disorders, particularly in the identification of blood cells such as neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils.

questionText: Which of the following is most commonly associated with febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reactions:
explanation: Febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reactions are most commonly associated with an immune response to leukocytes, which are white blood cells present in the transfused blood product. This reaction occurs when the recipient's immune system recognizes the leukocytes as foreign and mounts an immune response, leading to symptoms such as fever, chills, and nausea. The reaction is typically mild and self-limiting, but can be severe in some cases.

questionText: Which of the following is not a structural component of a typical virion:
options: Icosahedral symmetry Feedback: An intact viral particle typically consists of a nucleoprotein core, capsomeres making up the capsid, and a lipid envelope (absent in some viruses). The symmetry of a virus is usually icosahedral, or helical.
explanation: The nucleoprotein core is not a structural component of a typical virion, but rather the genetic material (DNA or RNA) surrounded by proteins, which is then enclosed by the capsid and lipid envelope.

questionText: The renal threshold is best described as:
options: Concentration at which a substance in the blood spills into urine
Concentration at which reabsorption first occurs
Concentration at which kidney can no longer filter the blood
Concentration at which kidney failure begins Feedback: The renal threshold is the maximum amount of a substance that the kidney can prevent from entering into the urine.
explanation: The renal threshold is the maximum concentration of a substance that the kidneys can reabsorb back into the bloodstream, preventing it from entering the urine. At this point, any excess substance will be excreted in the urine. This concept is crucial in understanding the concentration and excretion of various substances in the body.

questionText: An urticarial reaction is characterized by:
options: Blood in the urine Feedback: Urticarial transfusion reactions occur in up to 1% of transfusions. They are manifested by hives,rash, and itching. The transfusion may be resumed after successful administration of antihistamines.
explanation: An urticarial reaction is characterized by a rash and hives, which are manifestations of an allergic response. This reaction is distinct from other symptoms such as difficulty breathing or a rapid rise in temperature, which are indicative of more severe reactions. Urticarial reactions are typically treated with antihistamines.

questionText: On sheep blood agar Haemophilus influenzae may exhibit satellite formation around all but which of the following organisms:
options: Pneumococcus Feedback: Neisseria, Staphylococcus, and Pneumococcus produce enough V factor to allow H. influenza to grow on blood agar near their colonies. This property is utilized in the "satellite test" technique whereby minute colonies of Haemophilus are seen in the hemolytic zone surrounding a streak of Staphylococcus aureus on sheep blood agar, providing a presumptive identification of Haemophilus.
explanation: Neisseria, Staphylococcus, and Pneumococcus produce enough V factor to allow H. influenzae to grow on blood agar near their colonies, which is why they do not exhibit satellite formation around these organisms.

questionText: Adult Hematopoiesis occurs in:
options: All of the above Feedback: By the age of 18-20 years, active hematopoiesis is limited to the sternum, ribs, pelvis, vertebrae, and skull.
explanation: Adult hematopoiesis is indeed limited to the sternum, ribs, pelvis, vertebrae, and skull by the age of 18-20 years. This is because these sites provide a suitable environment for the production of blood cells, with a rich blood supply and a supportive bone marrow microenvironment. The proximal ends of long bones also contribute to hematopoiesis in adults, making all of the above options correct.

questionText: A simple check which can be employed to verify that hemoglobin and hematocrit values match would be:
options: Hemoglobin + hematocrit =3 Feedback: The hematocrit is equal to approximately 3 times the hemoglobin level.
explanation: The hematocrit is approximately 3 times the hemoglobin level because it represents the proportion of blood volume occupied by red blood cells, which contain hemoglobin. Therefore, if hemoglobin is multiplied by 3, it should approximate the hematocrit value, as the hematocrit is essentially the hemoglobin concentration multiplied by 3 to account for the volume of red blood cells.

questionText: How close the assayed value of an analyte is to its actual value is a reflection of:
options: Accuracy of the assay Feedback: Accuracy is defined as how close an assayed value is to the actual value of an analyte.
explanation: Accuracy in clinical laboratory medicine refers to the closeness of an assayed value to the actual value of an analyte. It is a measure of how reliable the results are, indicating the degree to which the results are unbiased and precise. In this context, accuracy is the reflection of how close the assayed value is to its actual value.

questionText: The primary mechanism responsible for glomerular filtration is:
options: Rate of blood flow through the kidneys

Hydrostatic differential in glomerular tufts Feedback: The hydrostatic pressure in the capillaries of the glomerular tuft drives the filtrate across their semipermeable membrane. The normal glomerular filtrate is similar in composition to the plasma, with the exception that molecules with a molecular weight of greater than about 15,000 are not filtered.
explanation: The primary mechanism responsible for glomerular filtration is the hydrostatic differential in glomerular tufts, which drives the filtrate across the semipermeable membrane. This process is driven by the higher hydrostatic pressure in the capillaries compared to the surrounding glomerular capsule. As a result, small molecules are filtered out of the blood and into the filtrate.

questionText: Which of the following best describes a minor crossmatch:
options: Reaction of donor cells with recipient serum
Reaction of donor cells with AHG
Reaction of recipient cells with AHG
Reaction of donor serum with recipientcells
